name: Scheuermann's kyphosis

card.summary: A structural rounded-upper-back condition of adolescence that people cite when explaining a stooped look, and whose bracing, exercise and surgical treatments can change upper-back posture.
card.aka: Scheuermann's disease, Scheuermann kyphosis, juvenile roundback
card.note: A medically diagnosed spinal condition; treatment decisions (bracing, exercise, surgery) are made with an orthopedic clinician.

quick.overview:
Scheuermann's kyphosis is a developmental condition in which several vertebrae in the upper or middle back grow wedge-shaped, producing a rigid forward rounding of the back. It usually becomes noticeable in adolescence and is the structural cause people point to when ordinary postural slouching does not correct itself on request.

For appearance, it matters because the shape of the thoracic spine sets the look of the shoulders, chest and head position. Clinical reviews describe bracing, dedicated exercise programs and, for larger curves, spinal fusion surgery as the ways the curve is managed, and note that cosmetic concern is itself one of the recognised reasons surgery is considered.
quick.how: Diagnosis is made by an orthopedic clinician from standing spine X-rays, where three or more adjacent vertebrae show at least 5 degrees of wedging. Milder cases are typically followed with observation, physical therapy and exercise programs such as Schroth-type approaches, sometimes with a brace during growth. Lifters and posture-focused communities discuss mobility and upper-back strengthening programs alongside a diagnosis, usually asking how the condition affects training.
quick.risks: Reviews describe back pain that can worsen with activity, a lifelong condition that can progress into adulthood in some people, and, for severe curves, effects on lung and heart function. Surgery carries recognised risks, with complication rates around 10 percent and reoperation in about 5 percent within five years reported in one summary. Lower-than-average bone density has also been described.

lead: Scheuermann's kyphosis (also called Scheuermann's disease) is a developmental spinal condition in which the front of several vertebrae grows more slowly than the back, giving them a wedge shape and producing a fixed forward curve of the upper or middle back. It is named after the Danish surgeon Holger Scheuermann, who described it in 1920 [1]. Unlike habitual slouching, the curve cannot be fully straightened voluntarily [1].

People in posture and physique communities mention it because it changes how the upper back, shoulders and neck sit, giving a rounded or 'hunchback' profile that can affect how tall and open the torso looks. Discussion threads on T Nation from the mid-2000s include lifters who report a diagnosis and ask how to train around it, and how programs aimed at rounded shoulders apply to them [2][3].

Clinical literature describes diagnosis by imaging and management by observation, exercise and physical therapy, bracing and, for larger curves, surgery. Reviews place its prevalence somewhere between about 0.4 and 10 percent, with higher rates in males [4][5].

chain: Wedged thoracic vertebrae form a rigid forward curve
Rounded upper back, forward shoulders and head position
Bracing, exercise or surgery change the curve and how the torso looks
angle.text: The condition shapes upper-back posture, so treatment that changes the thoracic curve changes how the shoulders, chest and head sit. Exercise programs, bracing during growth and, for large curves, fusion surgery are the options clinicians describe, and appearance concerns are one of the listed reasons surgery is considered.

infobox: About 0.4 to 10 percent; more common in males [1][5]
3 or more adjacent vertebrae with at least 5 degrees of wedging [5]

paras: In Scheuermann's kyphosis the vertebral bodies in the thoracic spine grow unevenly, so the back side of each affected vertebra outpaces the front. The result is a rigid, wedge-based curve that the person cannot consciously correct [1]. It is defined radiographically as three or more contiguous vertebrae with at least 5 degrees of anterior wedging [5]. The seventh and tenth thoracic vertebrae are among the most frequently involved [1].

Associated features described in the literature include a compensatory lower-back curve, tight hamstrings and, in some people, coexisting scoliosis [1]. Upper thoracic curves tend to be more visible, while lower thoracic curves tend to cause more pain [1]. The size of the curve does not reliably predict pain or quality of life [1].
The cause is not settled. Reviews discuss growth irregularities, mechanical stress, hormonal factors, genetic contributions and bone quality as candidates [4][5].

Because the curve sits in the thoracic spine, the visible effect is a rounded upper back, with shoulders and head often carried forward. A clinician distinguishes it from postural roundback, which is flexible and corrects with effort, by examination and standing X-rays [1][4].

Cosmetic appearance is named in the orthopedic literature as one of the indications that can contribute to a decision for surgery, alongside large curve size, pain, neurologic deficit and cardiopulmonary compromise [5].

Most patients are treated without surgery. A 2019 orthopedic review describes observation, anti-inflammatory medication and physical therapy as the usual approach, with a favourable prognosis for milder curves below about 70 degrees [5]. A 2023 review adds that dedicated exercise programs and brace type and duration have been refined in recent years [4]. Schroth-type exercise, originally developed for scoliosis, has been used for kyphosis too; a systematic review of Schroth trials found only one that enrolled Scheuermann's patients and rated the overall methodological rigor of the field as suboptimal [6].

Surgery is generally considered for thoracic curves above roughly 70 to 75 degrees, larger thoracolumbar curves, intractable pain, neurologic deficit, cardiopulmonary compromise or poor cosmesis, and is now usually done through a posterior-only approach [5]. Recovery involves lifting restrictions of six months to a year in one summary, with complications of about 10 percent and reoperation in about 5 percent within five years [1].

A long-term follow-up published in 1993 evaluated 67 patients diagnosed with Scheuermann's kyphosis (mean curve about 71 degrees) an average of 32 years later, using questionnaires, examinations, radiographs, pulmonary testing and trunk strength testing, and compared them with controls [7]. A 2022 prospective comparative study in northern Jordan assessed quality of life in patients with curves of 50 to 65 degrees treated conservatively or surgically [8]. Surgical series have reported results of posterior-only treatment with segmental shortening (the Ponte procedure) and of operative management in larger patient groups [9][10]. Reviews summarising this work are cited above [4][5].

On T Nation, users with a diagnosis have asked whether upper-back posture programs are suitable for them and how the curve affects future lifting [2][3]. Posts describe cost as a barrier to chiropractic care and ask for training alternatives [3]. These are individual accounts, and the clinical literature directs management to a treating clinician.

timeline.event: Long-term follow-up (mean 32 years) of 67 patients is published [7].
Ponte-procedure and operative series on posterior treatment are published [9][10].
AAOS review sets out indications and fusion-level selection [5].
Review notes advances in exercise, bracing and posterior-only surgery [4].

lore.intro: Lifters who have been diagnosed discuss the condition on T Nation, mostly asking how it interacts with training and posture programs [2][3].

claims.claim: Posture-correction programs can help a person with a diagnosed Scheuermann's curve
claims.believers: Forum users with a diagnosis ask whether programs aimed at rounded shoulders and forward posture are suitable for them, and some report using them [3].
claims.experts: Reviews describe dedicated exercise programs as part of non-operative treatment and note that evidence from Schroth-type trials is limited in rigor [4][6].

claims.claim: A rounded upper back is just slouching that can be corrected by willpower
claims.believers: This is the common assumption in posture discussions, where upper-back rounding is attributed to habit.
claims.experts: Orthopedic reviews describe Scheuermann's kyphosis as a rigid structural deformity that is not voluntarily correctable, distinct from flexible postural roundback [1][5].
